# Contributing

## Setup

Requires Node 24 and [Bun](https://bun.sh) 1.4.4, which runs the tests.

```sh
npm ci
npm run check
```

`npm run check` runs every stage in order and stops at the first failure; `node scripts/check.mjs <stage>` runs one.
Stages: `typecheck`, `unit`, `build`, `icons`, `copies`, `host`, `pack`, `forbidden`, `whitelist`, `actionlint`.

- `unit` runs against narrow fakes, and imports the real stock OpenCode binaries where they are installed
  (`test/unit/prover.test.ts`).
- `host` runs the built plugin on an embedded OpenCode host from `@opencode/sdk`, on each release in `TESTED_HOSTS`.
- `pack` installs the tarball it just built and loads both entries.
- `whitelist` checks `package.json` and `dist/` against the approved shape.

Stock binaries: set `OPENCODE_BIN_2_2_3` … `OPENCODE_BIN_2_2_6` to a stock `opencode` binary, or install
`@opencode/cli-<platform>-<arch>` for the release into a folder of its own. A stage that needs one skips when it is
absent. CI installs all four, so the import-id evidence runs on every push.

Before a release, work through [docs/live-check.md](docs/live-check.md) on one real machine.

## Install from a checkout

Only for development. Install the package into an OpenCode project from the folder, not from the registry:

```jsonc
{ "plugins": ["./opencode-boxd"] }
```

A published install is `opencode plugin add github:joe-broadhead/opencode-boxd#v0.1.0`.

## Rules

Read [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md). The short version: every machine change asserts its own permission, the guest must match
the laptop's OpenCode, the laptop ledger is the source of truth, and no check runs a real boxd machine.

## Releasing

Each release is the GitHub tag `v<version>`, where `<version>` is the `version` in `package.json`, and users install from
that tag. The release is one commit on top of a `master` head that CI passed, and the tag points at it. The release
workflow makes both, in GitHub Actions: nobody builds, commits or tags a release on their own machine, and no personal
key signs it.

While changes land, their notes go under `## [Unreleased]` at the top of `CHANGELOG.md`. Each earlier GitHub release is
a `## [x.y.z] - YYYY-MM-DD` heading below it, newest first, and the npm history stays last, under
`## Earlier releases on npm`.

1. On `master`, set `version` in `package.json` to the new version, and change every install spec in the README,
   `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `docs/` to `#v<version>` (`test/docs.test.ts` fails until they match). Then run
   `node scripts/changelog.mjs release`: it turns `## [Unreleased]` into `## [<version>] - <today>`, above the earlier
   releases, and refuses a CHANGELOG it cannot shape. Run `npm run check`.
2. Push that commit to `master`, and wait for CI to pass on it. A pull request's CI runs the Linux runners only; the
   push to `master` runs every runner, macOS too, and the release stands on that run.
3. Start the release with that commit's full sha:
   `gh workflow run release.yml --ref master -f sha=<full sha>`, or from Actions → release →
   Run workflow, on `master`.
4. Read the run's summary, then approve the `release` environment. The summary is on the run page, under the `stage`
   job: the tag, the parent and its CI run, the release commit and its tree, the sha256 of `SHA256SUMS` and the staged
   artifact's id, `SHA256SUMS` itself, and the notes. Open the release commit on `release/v<version>` and read them
   before approving: the approval releases exactly those bytes. Only the owner approves a release. Agents never approve
   one, never call the deployment-approval API, and never bypass a ruleset or the environment; the kit's scripts make
   only their own GitHub calls and refuse every other.
5. Check the published Release: not a draft, its notes, and every asset against `SHA256SUMS`.

`package.json` stays `"private": true`, so npm can never publish the plugin by accident; a GitHub install does not read
it, and `npm pack` still packs the release tarball. It is kept in its canonical form, `JSON.stringify(pkg, null, 2)` and
one newline: the kit tests check both in `npm run check`, as the release planner does.

The declaration is checked against what the provider serves. `npm run capture` (`scripts/capture-tools.mjs`, run by hand
through the signed-in OpenCode, never by CI) writes `test/fixtures/live-tools.json` and `test/fixtures/provenance.json`,
with the signed-in account's own values that some servers write into descriptions (Slack's "Your user_id: …") replaced
by placeholders such as `U00CURRENTUSER`; the drift check fails a committed capture that still holds one.
`scripts/check-drift.mjs` checks `jelly.tools`, `test/fixtures/tool-registry.json`, the skills and the docs against them,
offline, in the kit tests of `npm run check`. The release build runs it with `--release`, which also refuses a capture
more than 14 days old, unless `provenance.json` holds the owner's written waiver for exactly that capture:
`"waiver": { "listedAt": "<the capture's date>", "reason": "…", "approvedBy": "…" }` (a new capture drops it). A plugin
with no capture yet, or only a names-only one, releases with a warning on the run; one that serves only its own tools
says so with `"upstream": "none"` in the registry.

A plugin that declares sources (a top-level `sources` key in `package.json`, the source contract's declaration) releases
with its conformance report. Its `npm run conformance` runs the source contract's conformance kit and writes
`reports/conformance-report.json` (keep `reports/` out of git); `npm run check` runs it too. The release runs it again on
the parent in its own `conformance` job, which has no write token, and stops unless the run passes and the report's `ok`
is `true` for this version. The report becomes the Release asset `conformance-report.json`, listed in `SHA256SUMS`. A
plugin without `sources` has no report, and its release is unchanged.

Before the approval, the workflow:
- **plans:** refuses a run that is not on `master`, a sha that is not `master`'s head, a sha without a successful
  `ci.yml` push run with a successful job on every runner its push matrix names (macOS included), a `ci.yml` whose
  matrix runs macOS on a pull request or not on a push (the kit tests check it too), a version that is not `x.y.z`, a
  `package.json` that is not `"private": true` or not in its canonical form, a CHANGELOG whose newest release is not
  this version, a plugin that declares sources with no `conformance` script, a release that does not move forward from
  the last published Release, a leftover `release/v<version>` branch, a native run that did not build this sha on
  `master`, by hand, with success, and a missing `native_run` (or one given to a plugin that is not native);
- **builds**: refuses a failing tool drift check (`scripts/check-drift.mjs --release`, above), then builds `dist/` with
  `npm ci --ignore-scripts` and `npm run build`, with a read-only token, and writes the release files: `dist/`,
  `package.json` without its lifecycle scripts, and the vetted native manifest;
- **commits** them on a temporary branch `release/v<version>` at the parent, through GitHub's API with the workflow's token,
  so GitHub signs the commit (author `github-actions[bot]`, committer GitHub). This job runs no npm. It refuses a commit
  that GitHub does not verify, or whose parent or tree is not the one the files give;
- **verifies** on a fresh runner: the commit's identity, one parent on `master`, `package.json` exactly the parent's
  without the lifecycle scripts, only regular files in the allowed paths, no `package.json` under `dist/`, and a second,
  independent build of the parent (its own job) equal to the committed `dist/` byte for byte;
- **installs** the release commit with `plugin add` on each stock OpenCode host (2.2.3 to 2.2.7 and 2.3.0);
- **packs** the commit before installing anything, keeps that tarball and records its sha256, then runs the pack stage
  against a copy;
- **runs the conformance kit** on the parent, for a plugin that declares sources (above), and uploads only its report;
- **stages** the Release: verifies the attested native files, takes the conformance report of a plugin that declares
  sources from its job's artifact (exactly that one file, at most 256 KiB, nothing else), checks after every download
  that the staged tarball is the one the pack job kept (its sha256), writes `SHA256SUMS` and the notes (the version's CHANGELOG section), and shows them all in the run summary
  with the sha256 of `SHA256SUMS`.

A job either runs repository or dependency code (`npm ci`, the build, the pack stage, a host install) and has no write
token, or uses the API and runs only the kit's scripts on a fresh checkout, after checking that the release commit's
`scripts/` and `.github/` are the parent's. The first kind is not token-free: `actions/checkout` fetches with the job's
read-only (`contents: read`) token, and its post step and the artifact uploads run after repository code on the same
runner, so that code could reach a read-only token for this public repository and the runner's artifact token. Jobs
pass files as artifacts downloaded by the id the uploading job gave, and each is checked again on arrival.

After the approval, it downloads the staged artifact by the id the summary names, and refuses unless `SHA256SUMS` has
the sha256 the summary shows and every staged file matches it, the tarball is the one the pack job kept (its sha256),
every native file is the one the release commit's `manifest/native.json` pins, size and sha256, with each gzip holding
the pinned executable, and the conformance report is ok for this version. Then it checks everything again, creates the annotated tag
`v<version>` on the release commit (tagger `github-actions[bot]`, unsigned), checks the tag, creates the Release with the
notes, the tarball, the native files and `SHA256SUMS`, and deletes `release/v<version>`. The tag keeps the commit.

GitHub's signature and the bot identity show only that GitHub made the commit through its API for the workflow; anyone
with write access can make such a commit. What ties the release to `master` is its content: one parent CI passed, the
exact `package.json`, the allowed paths and the byte-for-byte rebuild. Never relax those because the commit is signed.

**A rejected, expired or failed run** leaves nothing behind: the `cleanup` job deletes `release/v<version>` when it points
at the parent or at that run's commit, and never touches another branch. No tag exists before the approval, so the
version is not burned: fix `master` and start again. If `cleanup` itself failed, the next run refuses until the branch
is deleted: `gh api -X DELETE repos/joe-broadhead/opencode-boxd/git/refs/heads/release/v<version>`.

**Resume.** If the run fails after creating the tag and before the Release is complete, start it again with the same `sha`. The plan finds the kit's tag on a release commit on that sha with no published Release, and resumes:
it makes no new commit, checks and installs the tagged commit, stages the files, and after a new approval reuses the tag
and adds what the Release lacks. Delete a draft Release a failed upload left first: the publish step refuses a draft.
Any other existing tag is refused: release the next version.

The repository's tag ruleset keeps a `v*` tag from being moved or deleted. A stray `v*` tag, one that never became a
Release, does not block later releases: only published Releases count, and drafts do not. Its version cannot be
released, so release the next one. To remove the tag anyway, an admin disables the `release tags` ruleset, deletes the
tag, and restores the ruleset exactly as it was.

**Known limit: a `v*` tag pushed by hand.** No ruleset limits who creates a `v*` tag, so anyone with write access can
push one by hand, pointing at any commit. Such a tag has no published Release, the forward-only check ignores it, and
Jelly installs only a published Release whose `SHA256SUMS` it verifies. But a user who installs
`github:joe-broadhead/opencode-boxd#v<x>` directly gets whatever that tag points at. Only the release workflow makes
release tags; never push one by hand.

The release kit is these files, the same in every plugin: `scripts/release-rules.mjs`, `scripts/release-commit.mjs`,
`scripts/release-github.mjs`, `scripts/check-release-shape.mjs`, `scripts/changelog.mjs`, `scripts/release-version.mjs`,
`scripts/release-pack.mjs`, `scripts/publish-release.mjs`, `scripts/attach-native.mjs`, `scripts/native-manifest.mjs`,
`scripts/tested-hosts.mjs`, `scripts/check-release-plugin-add.sh`, `scripts/check-drift.mjs`, `scripts/capture-tools.mjs`,
`scripts/release-kit.test.mjs`, `scripts/drift-kit.test.mjs` and `.github/workflows/release.yml`. `scripts/check-copies.mjs`
pins each of the scripts whole by its sha256, so a plugin whose copy differs from the family's fails `npm run check`:
change the kit in every plugin at once, with the new hashes. Do not re-run the older `apply-release-kit.mjs`: it writes
back the kit that could release only `v0.0.0`.

Each release has its own tag, and a Git install does not update by itself. To move to a newer release, remove the old entry with `opencode plugin remove github:joe-broadhead/opencode-boxd#v<old version>`, then add the new tag with `opencode plugin add github:joe-broadhead/opencode-boxd#v<version>`.

Or add the plugin to `opencode.json` instead, with the same spec:

```json
{ "plugins": [{ "package": "github:joe-broadhead/opencode-boxd#v0.1.0" }] }
```

# Security

## Supported versions

The latest GitHub release (`github:joe-broadhead/opencode-boxd#v<version>`) is supported.

## Reporting a vulnerability

Report a vulnerability through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting on
[joe-broadhead/opencode-boxd](https://github.com/joe-broadhead/opencode-boxd/security/advisories/new). Do not open a
public issue for a security problem.

## Data handling

- The plugin runs your own `boxd` CLI and stores no credential of yours: it never reads your boxd account, a token or a
  signed URL.
- On the machine, the guest helper generates a random password for that machine's own OpenCode server, keeps it at
  `/tmp/opencode-boxd/password` (mode 0600) on that machine only, and sends it nowhere else: only to the server's fixed
  loopback address. The laptop stores none of it.
- The ledger at `~/.local/share/opencode-boxd/` holds the session exports, a stored diff, the captured untracked files
  and the git record. It is the laptop's copy of the session. Its folders are mode 0700 and its files 0600, because an
  export is a full transcript.
- The guest OpenCode binds to `127.0.0.1` inside the machine. Nothing publishes that port.
- A work's laptop files stay inside the project or a folder named in the `allowedRoots` option. A harvest writes a file
  there only after the export is recorded, never outside both, and never through a symlink; when the host asks for a
  folder outside the project, it asks for the `external_directory` rule as well as the path rule, and `PATH_REFUSED`
  names that rule as its next step.
- Status and errors carry no token, code, signed URL or user content; `src/redact.ts` cuts a failure's reason to one line
  of at most 160 characters.

## Permissions

**Every tool is allowed by default.** The plugin inserts a block after each agent's base allow that allows all nine
tools, including the machine changes: with no rule of your own, an agent can create a billing boxd machine, start a
model run on it, save a snapshot and destroy the machine, without a prompt. The `access` option restricts that in one
line (`"ask-changes"` asks for every change, `"read-only"` denies them), and a per-tool rule does it for one tool.

What still holds without a prompt: a machine that idles hibernates, `boxd_sleep` always works, `boxd_drop` refuses
unless the laptop import is fresh and the tree can be accounted for, the ledger records a create before it runs, and a
read never wakes a machine (waking starts billing, so only a changing call does it).

`boxd_drop` destroys only what the laptop can account for: a proven import, a git repository, and no untracked or
ignored path. Everything else is refused, and hibernate keeps the disk. A plugin tool asserts its own permission inside
`execute`, because the host does not assert one for a plugin tool by itself.

## Scripts

A script calls the same tools through the `boxd.machines.tools` RPC, with no model. The tools RPC resolves the rule
before dispatch, from a prior explicit allow only: an `ask` is refused with no prompt and no call, a `deny` is refused,
and a saved "Always allow" does not authorize an ad-hoc script. A script's grant is a rule in config. Its reach is one
method at a time; a script cannot widen a rule, and it cannot reach the host's shell, file or network tools.

# Architecture

The plugin has one job: let one coordinating agent on a laptop drive 1 to 300 or more OpenCode sessions on boxd
machines, and keep every transcript on the laptop. [v1-design.md](v1-design.md) is the full design; this page is the
map of what the code does.

```
OpenCode (laptop)                         boxd machine oc-<work id> (fra or nyc)
┌───────────────────────────┐ boxd CLI ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
│ boxd_* tools ── runner ───┼────────▶ │ ~/.opencode-boxd/guest.py         │
│ watcher ── notices        │ ◀────────┤ opencode serve on 127.0.0.1:4096  │
│ status, cost, automation  │ JSON     │ /home/boxd/work/<work id>         │
└───────────┬───────────────┘ lines    └──────────────────────────────────┘
            └── ~/.local/share/opencode-boxd/v1/ (works/<id>/work.json, exports, patch, untracked, events.jsonl)
```

## The pieces

Each package fills one entry module, and `src/plugin.ts` builds them once, in order: runtime, import, ledger, watcher,
cost, the runs, then automation, the hooks and `/boxd-cleanup`. `src/ports.ts` and `src/services.ts` are the contract.

- **The runtime** (`src/exec/*`, `src/boxd/*`, `src/guest/*`, `guest/guest.py`): the one runner every child process goes
  through, the boxd CLI port with regions and by-id verbs, the guest port over the v1 helper, and the laptop's own
  `opencode` for session imports.
- **The ledger** (`src/ledger/*`): format 1 under `v1/`, one record per work, copy-on-write writes, a lock per work
  across processes, the index, and `events.jsonl` with its cursor. `src/import-v0.ts` imports the earlier ledger once.
- **The machine runs** (`src/fleet/machines.ts` and the files it names): ensure, resume, reassign and golden images,
  and the shared list-form runner.
- **The session runs** (`src/fleet/sessions.ts` and the files it names): submit, harvest, sleep, drop, exec and read,
  the selectors, and the in-process actions automation and `/boxd-cleanup` use.
- **The fleet view** (`src/fleet/status.ts`, `src/fleet/job.ts`, `src/fleet/model.ts`): `boxd_status` and `boxd_job`.
- **The watcher and notices** (`src/watch.ts`, `src/notices.ts`): the sweep, phase events, the event stream, and the
  notices to each work's coordinator.
- **Cost and cleanup** (`src/cost/*`, `src/automation.ts`, `src/hooks.ts`, `src/cleanup.ts`): rates and estimates, the
  budget, automatic harvest and sleep, the session hooks, and `/boxd-cleanup`.
- **The registry** (`src/tools.ts`): one table of twelve tools, with their schemas, classes, descriptions and the one
  place that asserts before a change. The tools RPC, the transform, the default rules, Jelly's declaration and status
  derive from it.
- **Status** (`src/status.ts`, `src/tui.ts`): one model for `/boxd-status`, the `/boxd` dialog and the status RPC.

## One runner for every process

Every child the plugin starts goes through `src/exec/runner.ts`:

- At most 12 boxd children at once for tool calls and reads; the background (the watcher, status's guest reads) uses at
  most 4 of them. `boxd_exec` has its own lane of 4, and the laptop's session imports a lane of 2, so at most 18
  children exist at once.
- Every child has an explicit timeout (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL 2 s later), the call's stop signal, and an 8 MiB output
  cap. Transcripts and files go to disk with `machine cp`, never through stdout.
- A machine change, or a helper action that changes the guest, holds that machine's lock, keyed by its boxd machine id.
  A call takes a slot for one child at a time and gives it back before it waits, so a wait never holds a slot.
- **Acting by id.** Before every change, `machine get` resolves `oc-<work id>` in its region; the call refuses `NOT_OURS`
  unless the id is the one the ledger recorded, and then acts on the id.
- **The read rule.** A read on a guest runs only for a machine that a listing at most 2 s old shows running, uses only
  the helper already on the machine, and never uploads a file or writes the ledger. So a read never wakes a hibernated
  machine, apart from one 2 s race that boxd's missing "exec without waking" leaves.
- The runner samples the event loop's delay while a call runs; status reports the worst of the last 5 minutes.

## The work tree and the file trip

Every work has two folders, both recorded in the ledger: the laptop folder it belongs to (the project by default), and
the guest's own `/home/boxd/work/<work id>`. A laptop path is never sent to the machine.

- `boxd_submit` checks each `files` entry (inside a root, not a symlink, within 8 MiB a file and 32 MiB a call), copies
  it up with `machine cp` before the prompt, and records name, size and sha256.
- `boxd_harvest` has the helper write each session's export on the guest, copies each one to a temp file beside the
  stored copy, checks its size and sha256 against the helper's report, and only then renames it into place; then it
  deletes and re-imports the session on this laptop, parents first. The patch and the untracked files take the same
  path. A copy that is cut off or has the wrong digest leaves the stored copy as it was.
- `boxd_drop` compares the guest's own session marks (each session's last message id and message count) with what the
  harvest stored, so a prompt that bypassed the plugin blocks the destroy too.

## Reading the fleet

`boxd_status` costs one all-region `machine list` (shared, and reused for up to 10 s), the machine limit (cached for
60 s), and guest reads only for works that are busy, starting or unknown, whose machine a listing at most 2 s old shows
running, and whose last read is older than 60 s. Those reads run in the background lane, at most 8 s each and 20 s for
the call; a work whose read misses the budget keeps its last phase, marked `stale`. An idle, ready or asleep work's guest
is never read by status, because an inbound exec resets the machine's idle clock. An idle work's phase changes only by
a change tool, which records it, or by its machine going to sleep, which the listing shows. A `machine list` that fails
is never a guest failure: the reads that needed it are not made (`kind: "listing-failed"`), each work keeps its last
known phase, marked stale, and status, the watcher and `boxd_job` still answer.

The answer is bounded: at most `limit` works in `attention` or `works`, worst first, with `more` for the rest, and more
than 3 works that share a reason and a code fold into one `groups` line. `since` answers from `events.jsonl`, so it
costs no guest read; a cursor older than the kept log answers the full view with `cursorExpired: true`.

`boxd_job` takes one listing at most 2 s old and reads each running work's guest once: an explicit job pays one reset of
an idle machine's idle clock, and status never does. `/boxd-status` and the dialog read no guest at all.

## The watcher and notices

The watcher runs a local tick every 60 s, with no CLI call: it reads the ledger's index and tails `events.jsonl` when the
file changed, so an event a change tool or another OpenCode process appended reaches the subscribers. While any open work
is busy, creating or starting (or idle inside automation's window), each tick is also a sweep: one all-region listing,
then one read-only `phase` read for each busy work the listing shows running. A phase change is appended to the event
log (`unreachable` after two failed reads in a row, `gone` after two listings in a row without the machine) and handed
to every subscriber in `seq` order; cost and automation subscribe. The sweep stops when nothing is busy, when the plugin
stops, and after three failed sweeps in a row, which status reports; the next status call starts it again.

A notice goes only to the work's root coordinator: the session that started or last drove the work from the model path,
found by walking `parentID` up from the calling session. It is checked again just before posting, and a session that is
gone, archived or now under another one gets no notice and is unsubscribed. Changes are coalesced per coordinator, at
most one notice a minute, at most 20 works named, with the cursor for the rest. A notice holds only the plugin's words:
work ids, phases, outcomes and codes from the table, never a guest's text. With `notices: "wake"` an idle coordinator
starts a turn; a wake the host refuses is posted once more as queue only.

## Cost

boxd bills a running machine for active CPU and resident memory, a machine in standby for resident memory, a hibernated
one for disk, and a deleted one nothing. An idle work costs about the same running or in standby, so the plugin sets
auto-suspend off and relies on hibernation:

1. **At creation**, at every `access` level: auto-hibernate after `autoHibernateMinutes` (2 h), `idle.ignore-outbound`
   off, and a `delete-after` lease only with `leaseDays`.
2. **Automation**, on the watcher's events, by one OpenCode process per laptop: a finished work is harvested and then
   hibernated after `autoSleepMinutes`, and so is an orphan whose coordinator is gone. A work waiting on a person is
   left. Nothing automatic ever drops. It runs at `access: "all"`, or with `automation: "on"`.
3. **What agents see**: `cost` and `cleanup` in `boxd_status`, one fleet line on the tail of a coordinator's request
   when the fleet changed (the system prompt is never touched, so the prompt cache holds), and an end-of-turn check
   that speaks only when money burns and automation will not act.
4. **What the person sees**: the Cost row in `/boxd-status`, `/boxd-cleanup` with a permission prompt per action, and
   an optional daily `budget`.

## Why the guest is not the session

A golden image is an image: booting one restores a disk, not a transcript, and an image reaches every work made from
it. So a transcript moves only by export and import, the laptop holds the newest copy, and no work's machine is ever
saved as an image. Model credentials never enter an image: a guest gets its key from a sealed, host-bound `boxd env`
secret that boxd injects at boot.

## Platform facts

Measured against the boxd CLI and OpenCode releases named in each item; [live-check.md](live-check.md) lists what to
measure again.

**OpenCode**

- `opencode session import --standalone` keeps the transcript's id on 2.2.3–2.2.7 and 2.3.0. A second import of an id
  already present answers `Session already exists`, exits 0 and changes nothing, so a harvest deletes the session
  first; `opencode session delete` of an absent id exits 1 with its not-found words, which the plugin reads as absent.
- `POST /api/session/<id>/prompt` takes `delivery: "steer" | "queue"`; the default is `steer`, which a running session
  takes at its next step boundary. `POST /api/session/<id>/interrupt` stops a run.
- A session's last run is `info.outcome` (`succeeded`, `failed`, `interrupted`) on `GET /api/session/<id>`, with the
  failure's structured error on the last `idle` message. The helper asks for one message:
  `?type=idle&order=desc&limit=1`.
- `opencode serve --hostname 127.0.0.1 --port 4096` reads `OPENCODE_PASSWORD` on 2.x: `/api/info` answers 401 without
  credentials and 200 with them. Port 4096 listens on `127.0.0.1` only.
- `opencode auth login` needs a login shell: `boxd machine exec --tty` exits silently, `boxd connect` then
  `opencode auth login` works.

**The boxd CLI** (0.2.29 and 0.3.3; the laptop CLI 0.3.5 for the verbs the design names)

- `machine get --json` prints the id, status, size, labels, `sharing`, `isolated` (the string `"yes"` or `"no"`), the
  idle bounds and `delete_after`. `machine list --json` lists every machine with its status, size and labels, but no
  `id` and no `isolated`.
- A missing machine is `error: VM '<name>' not found` on 0.2 and `error: no machine "<name>" in <region>` on 0.3, exit 1.
  The stderr table reads only those, anchored to the name and region asked, as missing; a hint that names another
  region is `elsewhere`, and anything else is `BOXD_FAILED`.
- Lifecycle strings: `running`, `starting`, `hibernated` (briefly `standby` after a hibernate), `standby`, `stopped`,
  and `destroyed` only as `remove`'s own answer.
- A create from a 9 GiB snapshot answered in about 1 s and was `running` at once. A client killed 1.2 s into
  `machine new` still left a running machine, which the next ensure adopts.
- `wake` keeps a configured auto-hibernate bound. With `idle.ignore-outbound off`, an inbound `machine exec` resets the
  idle clock; with it on, a machine hibernated while its outbound requests ran.
- Hibernation keeps memory and running processes; `stop` keeps only the disk.
- `machine cp` round trips are byte-exact, from stdin and to stdout alike.
- `manage usage --json` reports each machine's running, standby, hibernated and stopped seconds, its vCPU, RAM and disk
  hours, and the cost in micro-units of the organisation's currency (rates 39000 per vCPU-hour, 12000 per GiB-hour of
  RAM, 80 per GiB-hour of disk); it can lag by up to 25 minutes (`complete: false`), and is for owners and admins.
- boxd regenerates `/etc/profile.d/boxd-env.sh` at every boot with the account's `boxd env` values, so an image built
  without it still gets the key at boot.
- The stock image carries OpenCode 1.19.5; `opencode upgrade --major` and then `opencode upgrade <version>` pins a 2.x
  release, about 4 s each.

## The tools RPC

`boxd.machines.tools` is the family's v2 module, copied verbatim outside its plugin block: a script calls each tool with
no model, as a session and its agent. The rules decide: only a resolved `allow` runs, an `ask` is refused because no one
can answer it, and every change still asserts inside its own run.

# Configuration

## Options

All options go in the plugin entry in `opencode.json`, and every one is optional:

```jsonc
{
  "plugins": [{
    "package": "github:joe-broadhead/opencode-boxd#v0.1.0",
    "options": { "region": "auto", "size": "2x8", "notices": "wake" }
  }]
}
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `access` | `"all"` | What the plugin's own tools may do without asking: `"all"` allows everything, `"ask-changes"` allows the reads and asks for every change, `"read-only"` allows the reads and denies every change. A later rule of the user's still wins. |
| `allowedRoots` | `[]` | Absolute laptop folders a work may read and write besides the project. A path outside both is refused. |
| `allowUntestedHost` | `false` | Run on an OpenCode outside `>=2.2.3 <2.4.0`. Status then says the host is untested. |
| `region` | `"auto"` | Where a new work goes: `"auto"` picks the region with the most free machines after `keepFree`, preferring one that already has the golden image; or `"fra"` or `"nyc"`. |
| `keepFree` | `{ "fra": 0, "nyc": 0 }` | Machines `"auto"` leaves free in each region, such as the organisation's CI pool. |
| `size` | `"2x8"` | A new work's size: `"1x4"`, `"2x8"`, `"4x16"` or `"8x32"` (vCPU x GiB). |
| `git` | none | `{ "name", "email" }`: the guest's git identity for every new work. Never a token. |
| `goldenPrefix` | `"oc-golden"` | Golden image names are `<goldenPrefix>-<opencode version>-<size>`, such as `oc-golden-2.2.6-2x8`. |
| `goldenBase` | `"stock"` | What a golden build starts from: stock boxd, or a snapshot name in the region it lives in. A base that holds model credentials is refused; [images.md](images.md) gives the recipe. |
| `goldenSetup` | none | An absolute laptop path to a script, inside the project or an allowed root, run on every golden builder before the scrub. |
| `buildGolden` | `"auto"` | `"auto"` builds a missing golden image when a work needs it; `"never"` answers `GOLDEN_MISSING` instead. |
| `notices` | `"wake"` | How a work's change reaches its coordinator: `"wake"` posts a notice that starts an idle coordinator's turn, `"queue"` posts one that waits for its next turn, `"off"` posts nothing. At most one notice a minute per coordinator. |
| `autoHibernateMinutes` | `120` | The platform's idle bound, set on every new work machine at creation (30 to 1440). Auto-suspend is always off: standby bills resident memory too. |
| `automation` | `"auto"` | Whether the plugin harvests and then hibernates finished and orphaned works by itself: `"auto"` is on at `access: "all"` and off otherwise; `"on"` is your standing consent at every access level; `"off"` is never. It never drops anything. Consent is per OpenCode process, and the ledger is one per laptop: a process at `access: "all"` (or with `automation: "on"`) also harvests and hibernates the finished works another project created at `"ask-changes"`. |
| `autoSleepMinutes` | `10` | Idle minutes before automation harvests and hibernates a finished work; `0` turns that step off. Setting it is not consent. |
| `orphanHours` | `12` | A running, not busy work that no plugin call touched for this long is harvested and hibernated, when automation is on. |
| `leaseDays` | `0` | A `delete-after` timer of this many days on every new work machine, renewed on activity; `0` is off, because boxd deletes the machine whatever it holds, unsaved work included. |
| `budget` | none | `{ "daily", "action" }`: today's machine cost, in the organisation's billing currency, at which status warns (`"warn"`) or the calls that would make a machine run are refused (`"refuse"`, `BUDGET_REACHED`). Machine cost only: model spend is not measured in this release. |
| `costContext` | `true` | One short fleet line on the tail of a coordinator's request when the fleet changed, and the works list on a compaction; `false` turns both off. The system prompt is never changed. |
| `idleCheck` | `true` | The end-of-turn check that speaks only when money burns and automation will not act; `false` turns it off. |

An unknown option, a value out of its range, or a removed option stops the plugin with `OPTIONS_INVALID`; OpenCode's
plugin list shows why. The option `snapshot` is gone: a golden image is built by the plugin from stock. Remove
`snapshot`; set `goldenBase` only to build on a hand-made base without model credentials.

## Where the ledger lives

`~/.local/share/opencode-boxd/v1/`, a folder of mode 0700 whose files are 0600:

- `works/<work id>/work.json`: the record. The region, the machine name and its boxd machine id, the size and image,
  the laptop folder and the guest folder, the root session and the coordinator its notices go to, the last prompt, what
  was saved (each session's digest and its last message id and count), the last run, git, and the files moved in and
  out by name, size and sha256.
- `works/<work id>/exports/<session id>.json`: each harvested transcript, copied from the guest and verified.
- `works/<work id>/patch.diff` and `untracked/`: the tracked changes and the untracked files at the last harvest.
- `events.jsonl`: every phase change, one line each, with a sequence number that is `boxd_status`'s cursor. It keeps at
  least the last 5 MiB.
- `index.json`: a cache of each record's state, region, phase and `saved`, refreshed by modification time.

Every write is a temp file beside the old one, verified, fsynced and renamed over it; nothing is written in place, so a
crash leaves the old file. Two OpenCode processes on one laptop share the ledger through a lock per work.

The first start of this release imports the earlier `works/` ledger once into `v1/`, all or nothing, and adds only a
`works/README-MOVED-TO-v1/` note folder beside the old records.

## What the plugin relies on

- **The laptop is the source of truth.** A harvest copies each session's export from the guest with `machine cp`,
  checks its size and sha256 against what the guest reported, and only then renames it over the stored copy; it then
  deletes and re-imports the session on this laptop, parents first, so the laptop holds the newest transcript.
- **A transcript moves only between matching versions.** A call that moves a transcript compares the guest's OpenCode
  with this laptop's (`GUEST_VERSION`); reads work across versions.
- **A read never wakes a machine.** `boxd_status`, `boxd_job`, `boxd_read` and the watcher read a guest only when a
  listing at most 2 s old shows its machine running, never upload anything, and never write the ledger. `boxd_status`
  and the watcher never read an idle guest, because a read resets the machine's idle clock.
- **Every change acts on the machine id.** Before a change, `machine get` resolves `oc-<work id>` in its region and the
  call refuses `NOT_OURS` unless the id is the recorded one; then it acts on the id.
- **One runner owns every process.** At most 12 boxd processes at once for tool calls and reads, 4 for `boxd_exec`, and
  2 laptop imports; each with an explicit timeout, the call's stop signal and an output cap.
- **Status is bounded.** One `boxd_status` answers for 300 works with at most `limit` items, `more`, and repeated causes
  folded into `groups`.
- **Notices carry only the plugin's words:** work ids, phases, outcomes, codes from the table below, and a cursor. Never
  a guest's text.

## Errors

Every plugin error reads `CODE: What happened. Next step: What to do.`, with exactly one next step. A tool's result for
it is `{ "state", "error", "message", "next" }`, plus the facts its code carries, so a Code Mode program or a script
reads the same parts the model does. No error, log or status line contains a token or a signed URL.

### Warnings

A warning sits beside a result that succeeded, in `warnings`, `attention` and status; it is never a refusal.

- **`UNHARVESTED_SLEEP`**: The machine was hibernated before its last prompt was harvested. Next step: boxd_resume({ workId }), then boxd_harvest({ workId }).
- **`BUDGET_WARN`**: Today's machine cost has reached the budget's daily limit. Next step: Lower the cost: boxd_sleep({ select: "idle" }), then boxd_drop({ select: "saved-finished" }); or raise budget.daily.
- **`BUDGET_UNKNOWN`**: boxd's machine usage is for organisation owners and admins, so this sign-in cannot measure the budget; refuse acts as warn. Next step: Sign the boxd CLI in as an owner or admin to measure the budget, or remove the budget option.
- **`LEASE_EXPIRING`**: The work's delete-after lease ends within 24 hours, and boxd deletes the machine whatever it holds. Next step: boxd_harvest({ workId }) now; any change call for the work renews the lease.
- **`AUTOMATION_BLOCKED`**: The plugin's automatic harvest or sleep of this work failed at the step the message names. Next step: Read the code the message names, fix it, then boxd_harvest({ workId }) and boxd_sleep({ workId }).
- **`NO_MODEL_CREDENTIAL`**: No secret that OpenCode reads as a model provider key is set, so a work's first prompt will answer GUEST_AUTH_FAILED. Next step: Give works a model key: a sealed, host-bound boxd env secret (boxd env set <KEY> <value> --secret --domains <provider hosts>), a separately named secret per provider, or opencode auth login on one work's own machine after boxd connect.

# Golden images

Every work machine boots from a golden image: a boxd snapshot named `<prefix>-<opencode version>-<size>` in the work's
region, such as `oc-golden-2.2.6-4x16`, that holds this laptop's OpenCode and the guest helper, and nothing else. The
plugin builds these images itself, from a fixed recipe; you do not build one by hand.

- `boxd_ensure` builds the image it needs when it is missing (option `buildGolden: "auto"`, the default). A build for
  one region and size is shared by every call that needs it at once. With `buildGolden: "never"`, `boxd_ensure` answers
  `GOLDEN_MISSING` and names the `boxd_golden` call instead.
- `boxd_golden` builds, lists or prunes images. With no input it builds the default size in every region that lacks
  one; `region`, `size` and `from` choose; an image that exists answers `present` unless `rebuild: true`.
- The size comes from the image, so a work machine never needs a resize, and nothing reboots after a create.
- Snapshots do not cross regions, so each region has its own images.

## The recipe

1. **A builder machine**: `oc-gb-<region>-<size>-<rand>`, labelled `role=golden-builder`, with `--delete-after 2h` as
   a safety net, so it is removed even if the laptop goes away. It starts from stock boxd, or from the `goldenBase`
   snapshot when one is set.
2. **One exec on the builder**: upgrade OpenCode to this laptop's version (`opencode upgrade --major` from the stock
   1.x, then `opencode upgrade <version>`), check `opencode --version` and that the guest server asks for its password,
   install the guest helper in `~/.opencode-boxd/`, and run your `goldenSetup` script when one is set.
3. **The scrub**, the same whatever the base: stop `opencode serve`, and delete `/etc/profile.d/boxd-env.sh` (boxd writes
   it again at every boot), the guest password, the helper's exports, and `/home/boxd/work/`. The build refuses a base
   whose OpenCode database holds a session (`GOLDEN_BUILD_FAILED`: the base was a used machine, not an image) and a base
   that holds `~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json` (`GOLDEN_HAS_CREDENTIAL`, below).
4. **Save and remove**: `snapshots save` under the image's name in that region, then the builder is removed.

A build takes about one to two minutes. No step ever saves a work's machine as an image: a work's checkout, its session
database, its guest password and whatever its session wrote never reach another machine.

## Model credentials are never baked into an image

An image reaches every work created from it, and anyone in your boxd organisation who can boot it. A key stored in an
image could not be scoped or rotated per work, and would outlive its rotation in every image that holds it. So a build
refuses a base with an `auth.json`, whatever `goldenBase` says, with `GOLDEN_HAS_CREDENTIAL`.

Give works a model key in one of three ways, in this order:

1. **A sealed `boxd env` secret, bound to the provider's hosts** (recommended):

   ```sh
   boxd env set OPENCODE_API_KEY <key> --secret --domains <provider hosts> --scope private
   ```

   boxd injects it at every boot; the machine holds only a placeholder, and the real value is sent only to the
   provider's hosts. One rotation reaches every work.
2. **A separately named secret per provider or team**, such as `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` for one and `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` for
   another, with each work's `model` choosing the provider.
3. **The provider's own sign-in on one machine**: a person runs `boxd connect oc-<work id>` and then
   `opencode auth login` there (it needs a login shell). The credential then lives on that work's disk only, and goes
   when the work is dropped.

Before a build, `boxd_golden` looks at the account's secrets. When none is one that OpenCode reads as a provider key, the
build still succeeds, but its result carries `warning: "NO_MODEL_CREDENTIAL"` with these three ways, and `boxd_status`
repeats it: the third way happens after the build. A work with no credential answers `GUEST_AUTH_FAILED` at its first
prompt, with the same next step.

A provider may refuse a service-account key (one answered 403 `provider.auth`); use a key made for this, with a spending
limit, and rotate it if anyone leaves the organisation.

## Your own customisation

- **`goldenSetup`**: an absolute path to a laptop script, inside the project or an allowed root, that the builder runs
  before the scrub. Use it for tools, configuration or skills every work needs. It runs in every region the same way.
- **`goldenBase`**: a snapshot name to build from instead of stock, so a hand-made machine's customisations carry over.
  A base snapshot lives in one region only; `goldenSetup` is how the same customisation reaches the other region. The
  base is scrubbed like any other, and refused if it holds a session or an `auth.json`.

The builder's labels are captured into the image, and a restore inherits them under its own: works set `role=session`,
which overrides `role=golden-builder`. Anything else that selects machines by that label must know this.

## When the laptop's OpenCode changes

A laptop upgrade makes a new image name, so new works get the new image and open works keep the one they recorded.
`boxd_ensure` upgrades an open work's guest in place once its session is idle; until then the work stays usable for
reads and prompts, and a harvest answers `GUEST_VERSION`.

Images pile up, one per OpenCode version, size and region. `boxd_status({ include: ["images"] })` marks each one
`inUse` when an open work records it, and `boxd_golden({ prune: true })` removes the ones no open work records and that
are not the current version's. It never removes an image an open work records, because `boxd_resume` rebuilds from it.

# Jelly

Jelly reads the `jelly` section of `package.json` to show this plugin in its marketplace and to decide
what a Jelly may call.

## What it declares

- **`tools`** — all twelve, by their permission action, with the effect the default rules give: every one of them
  `allow`, the three reads and the nine changes alike. 12 tools are declared (3 read-only): `boxd_status`, `boxd_job`
  and `boxd_read` are the reads.
- **`skills`** — `boxd`.
- **`signIns`** — empty. The plugin has no sign-in of its own: it runs your `boxd` CLI, which you sign in to with
  `boxd auth login`, and Jelly cannot show that sign-in on the card. `/boxd-status` shows it as its first row, **boxd
  CLI**, with `boxd auth login` as the next step when the CLI does not answer.
- **`icon`** — `assets/icon.svg`, boxd's own mark: boxd.sh's `favicon.svg`, unchanged, on a rounded tile in boxd.sh's page colour #0a0c12 (`opencode.vendor.mark` is `true`).
- **`cost`** — the line Jelly shows on the plugin's review before it installs, in the plugin's own words, saying what
  it costs with boxd: "boxd bills each plugin machine: compute and memory while running, disk while hibernated, until
  boxd_drop. boxd_golden and boxd_ensure may make a short-lived builder. At access Allowed, finished works are
  harvested and hibernated after 10 idle minutes by default; else only with automation "on"." It changes nothing Jelly
  allows. Jelly keeps the line to 300 characters.
- **`contributes`** — one setting, `access`, the option of the same name, as a choice of three: **Allowed** (`all`, the
  default), **Ask before changes** (`ask-changes`) and **Read only** (`read-only`), with Jelly's own line for each.
  Jelly draws it as a choice and saves only one of the three; a Jelly that does not know declared choices yet refuses
  the whole declaration. No home feed, widget or work kind.

`/boxd-cleanup` confirms each cleanup action with a permission prompt for the person: at **Allowed** through the
command's own action `boxd_cleanup`, which the default rules set to ask at every level; it is a command action, not a
tool, so it is not in `tools`.

Every tool the plugin registers is declared: the twelve tools are the plugin's own, and `test/unit/jelly.test.ts` fails
when a tool in `src/tools.ts` is missing from `jelly.tools`, so a release cannot add an undeclared one.

## What Jelly does with it

Jelly applies the `access` setting itself, from the declared `readOnly` of each tool: at **Allowed** (the default) all
twelve run without a prompt; at **Ask before changes** `boxd_status`, `boxd_job` and `boxd_read` run and the nine
changes ask; at **Read only** the three reads run and the nine changes are denied. A read-only helper is never given one
of the nine changes. The plugin's own guards that do not depend on a prompt hold in Jelly too: `boxd_drop` refuses a machine the
laptop cannot account for, and `boxd_sleep` always works.

The plugin's automation follows the same choice. At **Allowed** it harvests a finished work and then hibernates it after
`autoSleepMinutes` (10 by default), by itself. At **Ask before changes** and **Read only** it does neither, because a
change there either asks or does not run, and automation can do neither; only the person's own `automation: "on"` in
the plugin config, their standing consent, turns it on there. The idle bounds set when a machine is created apply at
every level, and nothing automatic ever drops a work.

Jelly's shared rules for every plugin of the family, word for word:

<!-- family-block:start -->
- At Allowed (`all`), the default, every tool runs without asking, declared or not, whatever its `effect`.
- At Ask before changes (`ask-changes`), a `readOnly` tool runs, and every other tool asks first, including a tool this plugin does not declare.
- At Read only (`read-only`), a `readOnly` tool runs, and every other tool is off, including a tool this plugin does not declare.
- A declared `effect` of `allow` changes nothing: the tool follows the access choice and its `readOnly`.
- A declared `effect` of `ask` makes the tool ask at Ask before changes, even when it is `readOnly`, and changes nothing at Allowed or Read only.
- A declared `effect` of `deny` turns the tool off at Ask before changes and at Read only, and changes nothing at Allowed.
- An action listed in `asks` asks first at Ask before changes and at Read only, and never at Allowed.
- A tool named with one `*`, such as another account's `plaud-*.get_file`, follows the same rules as a tool named in full.
- A choice the person makes for one tool wins over the access choice and the declared `effect`.
- jelly leaves out a key it does not know at the top level of the `jelly` block, and reads the rest.
- jelly refuses the plugin for a key it does not know inside anything it reads, such as a tool, a sign-in or a setting.
- jelly refuses the plugin, with one plain line, when `requires` names a field or a feature it does not read.

# Scripting

Every boxd tool is a method of the `boxd.machines.tools` RPC, so a script calls it with no model, as a session and the
agent it names. A script's grant is a rule in config: only a resolved `allow` runs, an `ask` is refused because no one
can answer it, and a `deny` runs nothing.

The session is created for the script with an agent (`opencode api post /api/session -d '{"title":"…","agent":"build","location":{"directory":"/path/to/project"}}'`, with `data.id` kept). The body is
`{"input":{"sessionID":"<id>","input":{…}}}`; both keys are required, and no other key is allowed. Give the project as the session's `location`: a session made without one belongs to the service's default location, where the project's agents may not exist, and each call then fails `Agent not found`.

```sh
opencode api post /api/rpc/boxd.machines.tools/boxd_job -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"<id>","input":{"workId":"review-api"}}}'
```

`describe` takes no input, or a session, and lists every method with its class and — given a session — the permission the
call would get:

```sh
opencode api post /api/rpc/boxd.machines.tools/describe -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"<id>"}}'
```

A plugin-owned method's result is the method's output object, as `describe` gives its schema: for boxd, the JSON the
tool itself returns, with a `state` on every answer. `text` is what the model path would show.

## Watching a fleet

`boxd_status` answers for the whole fleet in one call: `counts` by phase, each region's machine headroom, the works that
need a decision (`attention`, worst first, at most `limit`, with `more` for the rest), repeated causes folded into
`groups`, and the `cost` and `cleanup` blocks. It never wakes a machine and never reads an idle guest. Its `cursor`,
passed back as `since`, answers only the works that changed since; a cursor older than the kept event log answers the
full view with `cursorExpired: true`, so a gap is never mistaken for "nothing changed".

```sh
opencode api post /api/rpc/boxd.machines.tools/boxd_status -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" \
  -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"<id>","input":{"since":1842,"limit":50}}}'
```

A script's own session gets no notices: notices go to the coordinator that last drove a work from the model path. A
script names one with `notify` on `boxd_submit` (a session id, or `false` to clear it), and a submit without `notify`
leaves an earlier subscription in place.

## Many works in one call

`boxd_ensure`, `boxd_submit`, `boxd_job`, `boxd_harvest`, `boxd_sleep`, `boxd_resume` and `boxd_drop` take
`works: [...]`, 1 to 300 items, and answer `{ state, counts, results }` with one result per item in input order. `state`
is `done`, `partial`, `failed` or `cancelled`. A list call has a bound: an item still `creating` or `starting` when it
runs out answers that state, and an item that never started answers `cancelled` with `started: false`; both carry the
same `next`, which only waits and converges. Use one list call rather than many single calls at once.

```sh
opencode api post /api/rpc/boxd.machines.tools/boxd_ensure -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" \
  -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"<id>","input":{"works":[{"workId":"api-a","repo":"https://github.com/o/a"},{"workId":"api-b","repo":"https://github.com/o/b"}]}}}'
opencode api post /api/rpc/boxd.machines.tools/boxd_job -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" \
  -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"<id>","input":{"works":["api-a","api-b"]}}}'
```

`boxd_sleep`, `boxd_harvest` and `boxd_drop` also take `select` instead of `works`, resolved against a fresh listing and
the ledger; `dryRun: true` lists the matches and changes nothing:

```sh
opencode api post /api/rpc/boxd.machines.tools/boxd_sleep -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" \
  -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"<id>","input":{"select":"finished","dryRun":true}}}'
```

## Methods

| Method | Class | Runs when |
|---|---|---|
| `boxd_status` | read | allowed |
| `boxd_job` | read | allowed |
| `boxd_read` | read | allowed |
| `boxd_ensure` | write | the agent or session allows `boxd_ensure` |
| `boxd_submit` | write | the agent or session allows `boxd_submit` |
| `boxd_harvest` | export | the agent or session allows `boxd_harvest` (it writes this laptop) |
| `boxd_sleep` | write | the agent or session allows `boxd_sleep` |
| `boxd_resume` | write | the agent or session allows `boxd_resume` |
| `boxd_reassign` | write | the agent or session allows `boxd_reassign` |
| `boxd_golden` | write | the agent or session allows `boxd_golden` |
| `boxd_exec` | write | the agent or session allows `boxd_exec` |
| `boxd_drop` | destructive | the agent or session allows `boxd_drop` |

A class is the worst thing the method does; it never decides whether a call runs. The rules do.

## Files in and out

`boxd_submit` takes `files` to copy data to the machine, and `boxd_harvest` takes `files` to copy results back. A path is
relative to the work tree; a laptop path must be inside the project or a folder in `allowedRoots`, and a symlink is never
followed. The caps are 8 MiB a file and 32 MiB a call, and the ledger records each file's name, size and sha256, never
its content.

A worked example: summarise the bookmarks a previous step saved, and bring the summary back.

```sh
# 1. One work, with the laptop folder it belongs to. It answers when the guest's OpenCode is up.
opencode api post /api/rpc/boxd.machines.tools/boxd_ensure -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" \
  -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"<id>","input":{"workId":"bookmarks"}}}'

# 2. The data in, then the prompt. The model reads data/bookmarks.json, not a pasted list.
opencode api post /api/rpc/boxd.machines.tools/boxd_submit -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" \
  -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"<id>","input":{"workId":"bookmarks","text":"Read data/bookmarks.json and write SUMMARY.md: one line per site, grouped by topic.","files":[{"from":"bookmarks.json","to":"data/bookmarks.json"}]}}}'

# 3. Later: the outcome, then the transcript and the summary, then the machine down.
opencode api post /api/rpc/boxd.machines.tools/boxd_job -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" \
  -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"<id>","input":{"workId":"bookmarks"}}}'
opencode api post /api/rpc/boxd.machines.tools/boxd_harvest -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" \
  -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"<id>","input":{"workId":"bookmarks","files":["SUMMARY.md"]}}}'
opencode api post /api/rpc/boxd.machines.tools/boxd_drop -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" \
  -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"<id>","input":{"workId":"bookmarks"}}}'
```

`boxd_job` answers `state: "idle"` with `outcome: "completed"` when the model finished. The harvest makes the work
`saved: "fresh"`, and the drop succeeds because `SUMMARY.md` came back at the digest the guest still has; a file that
was never harvested keeps the refusal (`UNTRACKED`).

Two more reads help a script without a harvest:

```sh
opencode api post /api/rpc/boxd.machines.tools/boxd_read -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" \
  -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"<id>","input":{"workId":"bookmarks","path":"SUMMARY.md"}}}'
opencode api post /api/rpc/boxd.machines.tools/boxd_exec -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" \
  -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"<id>","input":{"workId":"bookmarks","command":["git","status","--short"],"timeout":30}}}'
```

`boxd_exec` is a change, because a command can do anything; each argument reaches the remote shell exactly as given.
When the work's machine runs out of room, `boxd_reassign` moves an unstarted work's machine to a new id, and
`boxd_golden` builds or prunes the golden images:

```sh
opencode api post /api/rpc/boxd.machines.tools/boxd_reassign -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" \
  -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"<id>","input":{"from":"spare-1","to":"bookmarks-2"}}}'
opencode api post /api/rpc/boxd.machines.tools/boxd_golden -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" \
  -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"<id>","input":{"region":"nyc","size":"4x16"}}}'
```

If the host asks for permission to touch a folder outside the project, allow it with the `external_directory` rule as
well as the path rule:

```jsonc
{ "permissions": [
  { "action": "external_directory", "resource": "/srv/work/*", "effect": "allow" },
  { "action": "read", "resource": "/srv/work/**", "effect": "allow" },
  { "action": "edit", "resource": "/srv/work/**", "effect": "allow" }
] }
```

A refusal that names `permission.rejected: external_directory` is fixed by that rule, and by naming the folder in the
plugin's `allowedRoots` option.

## Restricting one agent

To let one agent run a script that harvests, give that agent its own rule:

```jsonc
{ "agents": { "harvester": { "permissions": [{ "action": "boxd_harvest", "resource": "*", "effect": "allow" }] } } }
```

Every tool is allowed by default (the plugin's `access` option is `"all"`), and a script gets the same default: the
tools RPC resolves a rule before dispatch, and the default allow is that rule, so a script can call every method. To
restrict a script, set `access` to `"ask-changes"` (an `ask` is refused, because no one can answer it) or
`"read-only"`, or give the script's agent its own `deny` rule — the script's grant is a rule in config.

## The location

Run the command in the project whose agent you mean, and send the call to that location explicitly:

```sh
opencode api post /api/rpc/<id>/<method> -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" -d '{…}'
```

Without it the call goes to the service's default location and fails `rpc.unavailable` if the plugin is not loaded
there. The HTTP equivalents are the `location[directory]` query parameter and the same header. `describe` reports the
`location` that answered and a `locationHint`.

A location unloads after OpenCode's idle timeout. If a scheduled script gets `rpc.unavailable` from a location that was
loaded before, send the call again once: the request loads the location. Jobs keeps its own location loaded.

## Refusals

A call the RPC refuses before the method runs is the RPC error `failed`, with `data: { code, next }`:

| Code | When | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `PERMISSION_DENIED` | the rule resolves to ask, or a deny hides the method | add an allow rule for the action to the session's agent or to the session |
| `SESSION_UNKNOWN` | OpenCode does not know the session in this location | create the session in the location you mean, and pass its id |
| `SESSION_AGENT_REQUIRED` | the session names no agent | create a session that names an agent |
| `TOOL_UNAVAILABLE` | OpenCode does not list the method's tool now | call `describe` to see the methods there are |

A method that ran and refused answers with its output, not an RPC error, in the same shape as a success: `{ "state":
"<state>", "error": "<code>", "message": "<what happened>", "next": "<the one next call>" }`, with `workId`, `machine`
and `region` when the call named a valid work, and the facts its code carries: `field` (`NAME_INVALID`), `paths`,
`count` and `kind` (`UNTRACKED`), `limit` per region (`MACHINE_LIMIT`), `progress` (`LEDGER_IMPORTING`), `uncertain`
(`CANCELLED`), and `today`, `daily` and `currency` (`BUDGET_REACHED`). `state` is `refused`, `failed`, `unreachable`,
`busy`, `starting`, `gone`, `asleep` or `cancelled`, so a loop reads `state` on every answer. The codes a script meets
most:

| Code | When | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `LEDGER_IMPORTING` | the import of earlier works is not complete yet | the same call again in a few seconds |
| `NOT_OURS` | no open work has that id, or its name now points at another machine | `boxd_ensure` for an unknown id; otherwise look at the machines the message names |
| `MACHINE_LIMIT` | no region has room | the other `region` when it has room, or free machines with `boxd_drop` or `boxd_reassign` |
| `SESSION_BUSY` | the session is running and the call needs it idle | wait for the notice or `boxd_status`, or `mode: "interrupt"` |
| `NOT_SAVED` | drop without a fresh harvest, or the guest moved on since it | `boxd_harvest`, then drop again |
| `RUN_FAILED`, `GUEST_AUTH_FAILED` | the session's last run failed | read `lastText`; fix the credential for an auth failure; then `boxd_submit` again |
| `BUDGET_REACHED` | the daily budget is reached with `action: "refuse"` | sleep and drop finished works, or raise the budget |

Every other code the plugin raises is in `docs/configuration.md`, with its one next step.

Known limit: a saved "Always allow" answer from an earlier session is not part of the agent and session rules, so it
does not authorize an ad hoc script. A script's grant is a rule in config.
